description: Memory is not a library of drawers. It is a living network of neurons that strengthen, rebuild themselves and sometimes get it wrong.

hero.hook: A memory is not a file: it is a path the brain has learned to walk again.

blocks.text: We often imagine memory as a hard drive. In reality it is a living network. Billions of **neurons**, the cells of the nervous system, reconnect, strengthen or weaken according to what we live through.
Nothing is stored in a single place. A memory is a trace spread across the network, fragile at first, sturdier after sleep, and always rebuilt a little whenever we recall it.

The contact point between two neurons is called a **synapse**, the junction where the nerve signal crosses. The human brain holds roughly **86 billion** neurons and more than **100 trillion** synapses.

blocks.caption: The hippocampus plays a central role in forming memories

blocks.text: When a piece of information is repeated or tied to a strong emotion, the same neurons fire together. Their link becomes easier to trigger: this is [[long-term potentiation]], the lasting strengthening of synapses. The more a circuit is used, the “wider” the path becomes. A memory is therefore not a filed object but a **trace** in the network.
The storage capacity of the brain is estimated at around **2.5 petabytes**, the equivalent of millions of hours of video. But it is not a disk: it is living tissue that keeps reorganizing itself.

The **hippocampus**, a small structure in the [[temporal lobe]], the region behind the temples, does not keep memories forever. It receives them, **encodes** them, turns them into a memory trace, then passes them out to the **cortex**, the outer layer of the brain. That transfer is called **consolidation**.
It happens mainly during **sleep**. Without a working hippocampus, you can live in the present moment but you no longer fix new conscious memories. You stay stuck in a present with no recent past.
Patient **H.M.**, operated on in 1953, formed no new memories. Yet he got better every day at drawing in a mirror, without remembering that he had ever tried: his memory for movement was intact.

sections.title: The hippocampus, station master of memory

blocks.text: Recalling a memory is not replaying a video. Every time you pull it out, it becomes **malleable** again, open to change. Our mood of the moment, something we have just learned, or a simple suggestion can alter it before it is “saved” again.

The psychologist **Elizabeth Loftus** showed that **false memories** can be planted with nothing more than leading questions. Hence today's caution about eyewitness testimony: in perfectly good faith, the brain fills in the gaps.

Memory for facts and for episodes of life, the kind you can tell a story about, runs mainly through the hippocampus. [[Procedural memory]], the kind used for cycling or swimming, depends instead on the **cerebellum**, a structure at the back of the brain, and on other, older structures.
That is why some amnesic patients forget their own name but can still play the piano. Memory is not one single drawer: it is a mosaic of systems.
A memory is a dynamic trace: synapses strengthened, consolidated above all at night, and rebuilt at every recall. It is never a frozen file.
